We will support it and vote for it in due course, brother. I want to take this opportunity to say a few things about DEVCO and just where the Government is headed in Cape Breton with DEVCO.
There was a time when the DEVCO workforce was up around 6,500 employees. That was in 1965. Over the years the workforce has been eroded to 3,400 employees at present.
DEVCO had two arms. There was the coal mining arm and the industrial development division. That concept placed DEVCO in the picture of economic development in Cape Breton. In fact, DEVCO not only dealt with the coal mining operations on the island, it was also plugged into the diversification of the economy of Cape Breton. That seemed to be a proper approach.
What has happened now, of course, is that the Government established ACOA. The industrial development division of DEVCO has been put into Enterprise Cape Breton and it will now go under ACOA. ACOA will be administered by a Minister whose head office is here in Ottawa. The headquarters of ACOA will be in Moncton, New Brunswick. However, the major decision-making will be centralized here in Ottawa. DEVCO will simply be the coal mining operation.
At present there are three coal mines under the jurisdiction of DEVCO that need development work. We know the Government inherited DEVCO from the private sector. It was originally DOSCOE. The private sector could not make enough money. It never really invested in modernization of the operation and so the company left the shores of Cape Breton. The Government of the day had to save the jobs and avert disaster in Cape Breton. That is how it inherited DEVCO. It was not a planned initiative by the Government to enter the market-place. There was no planning to it. It was the private sector defaulting on its responsibility to the community, not living up to its social responsibility in Cape Breton, and pulling out. Like so many other Crown corporations, it is a history of the failure of the private sector, and the inability of Governments to hold the private sector responsible for their actions in a community. That is the history of DEVCO and it is now being sheared off and set up.
The question which the people of Cape Breton, the workers at DEVCO, have in their minds is: What is the long-term aim of the Government? What is the agenda?
Does it have one?

It has. Every time the Government says it is not going to do something, it is going to do it. It said it was not going to privatize Air Canada, and we know what happened. The Government's "no" means "yes".
Cape Breton Development Corporation Act
In this particular case the Government said it has no intention of selling off DEVCO to the private sector. We know that is the hidden agenda, and the people of Cape Breton are concerned. The workers at DEVCO are concerned. They know that there is a private operator in Pictou County called Westray. They are establishing a coal mine operation in Pictou County, Nova Scotia. The people of Cape Breton are concerned about what will happen once Westray is established. Of course they have probably already approached ACOA hats in hands for some hand-outs. I understand it is $75 million. You notice how these capitalists operate? They are all against government involvement in business. They want nothing to do with that. They want no regulations. They want governments off their backs. I hear it all the time. They condemn people who are on welfare. The John Bullochs of this world are all against the unemployment insurance program and our other social programs. They say they are disincentives to work.
However, why is it not a disincentive for the Corporation to go hat in hand to the Government for a $75 million hand-out? That is what is happening. They have a proposal before ACOA for $75 million. Therefore, on the one hand the Government will fund the establishment of coal mines in Pictou County in Nova Scotia while, on the other hand, setting DEVCO up by sharing it off and leaving it in left field.
We can see what will happen. DEVCO will be squeezed, it will not be advanced the money it needs to develop its mines. There will be no marketing for its coal and no money for research and development.

Cape Breton Development Corporation Act
That is the foundation of DEVCO's present existence. Sixty per cent of its production goes there. God knows, it has been a declining production over the years. Surely, we are not going to let happen to DEVCO what we let happen to Sysco with respect to the production of railway lines.

Member would support.

Member to find the answer to that question and provide it to him at a later date.

May 17, 1988

National Health and Welfare has entered the House. He might want to participate in the debate since it concerns pension and pension reform. Cape Breton Development Corporation Act

Member that many of these individuals are being told by senior management people that they will have to wait not one day, not two weeks, not three weeks, not one month, but maybe five years before their claim can be adjudicated. and economic opportunities. Coal mining in Nova Scotia is one of those opportunities.

Everyone knows that one of the dangers for coal miners, one which they live in constant fear of, is black lung disease. The present regulations provide for coal dust levels of two parts per million. However, in actual fact it is somewhere up around six parts per million-I am getting a signal that I am being a bit conservative-small "c" conservative, Mr. Chairman.
I am being signalled that it is eight parts per million in reality. Can the Parliamentary Secretary give us a commitment, since he is in a committing mood here today, that in fact greater resources will be directed toward bringing the levels of coal dust in the mines closer to the two parts per million that we have been unable to achieve so far?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
speechtext: I can give the Hon. Member this assurance. If we can get on with this stage of the Bill and increase the working capital limits for DEVCO that the management of DEVCO will have whatever pressure I can lend with respect to achieving that goal. corporation together with other institutions has been expending approximately that much on an annual basis, with some promising results.

Member raises. When funds are necessary, as has been the practice in the past, those funds will be available in the future. The well-being and the efficiency of DEVCO and coal mining in Cape Breton is very important to all of us, and in that sense I can certainly give the Hon. Member that understanding.

Some of the mines are in need of upgrading, for example, the Lingan mine facility and the Donkin-Morien mine. Could the Parliamentary Secretary be more specific. Does he think $25 million is enough? I wish to return to the question of employment at the Cape Breton Development Corporation. The question of a mine in Pictou County is one thing. Since the Government came into power there have been approximately 600 jobs lost at the Cape Breton Development Corporation. As

the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond has stated, the number of employees is down to 3,400.

Parliamentary Secretary knows, that industry is a cornerstone industry and it cannot afford to have further job reductions.

Perhaps that speaks loudly for the urgency of naming a new president and chief operating officer, a matter which I hope will happen within the next several days. The situation is a very serious one. speechtext: that Bill C-127, an Act to amend the Cape Breton Development Corporation Act, be read the third time and passed.

Mr. Speaker, I will be brief, because I think this Bill is a good one. However, a great deal needs to be done to the Cape Breton Development Corporation, but as far as it goes, I think this Bill can be supported.

May 17, 1988
Cape Breton Development Corporation Act
I listened to my friend from Nickel Belt speak at second reading stage. I was surprised at the strident position that he and his Party are now taking with respect to supporting the Cape Breton industrial development division of the Cape Breton Development Corporation. We certainly could have used that support from his Party last week when this came up for a vote and members of the New Democratic Party chose to support Bill C-103 which unequivocally, without hesitation or remorse and without afterthought completely terminated and absolutely abolished the industrial development division of DEVCO.
My friend and colleague from Cape Breton-East Richmond and I realized that that abolishment was in the Bill, and we had been speaking long and hard on the injustice of doing away with the industrial development division. Certainly our Party took the position that this was completely unjustified.
The Cape Breton Development Corporation legislation was brought forward in 1967. The legislation came about because of the will of the Canadian people, through the Members of Parliament of the time. The economy of Cape Breton was in such a difficult position that not only did the coal industry in Ccipc Breton hsve to be strengthened snd perhsps diversified but as well a development agency had to be set up to bring new jobs into the Cape Breton area.
That was the situation in 1967. The economy of Cape Breton is really no better off right now. In fact, the number of jobs in the coal industry has decreased since this Government took office. The Government has closed two heavy water plants, despite the assurance of the then Minister of Energy and now President of the Treasury Board (Miss Carney) that these heavy water plants would not be closed until alternate employment could be provided. However, these two plants were closed.
The Sydney steel plant in Cape Breton has reduced employment, and even though the Government seems to have approved the second phase of the modernization of Sydney Steel, this program is being delayed again and again, to the extent that one really wonders about the commitment of the Government to actually see this program brought forward.
There has been some encouragement with respect to the special investment tax credit and there has been an indication that certain industries will be locating in Cape Breton, but the actual number of jobs that have been committed to by industries starting in industrial Cape Breton has been a small fraction of the jobs that we lost. Not only have we lost jobs in the Crown corporations, but because of the downturn in the economy in industrial Cape Breton, an area with about 120,000 people, we lost other jobs as well as regional companies decided that they did not want to maintain offices in industrial Cape Breton and went to areas like Halifax. Jobs have been disappearing, to the detriment of the economy.
This Government has said that it will get the private sector to do it, that the private sector should be at the forefront of regional development. That has not been the case, however.
We have seen no evidence of that at all. In fact, in the recent annual report of the Small Businesses Loans Act, a report which was over a year late, we saw that all of Atlantic Canada, four of the 10 provinces of Canada, only received 6 per cent of the total business investment loan money available under the Small Businesses Loans Act which was passed by this Government.
The chartered banks are not allocating the money which the Government has guaranteed they will not lose. If these loans are not repaid, the chartered banks are guaranteed to receive 85 per cent of the money back from the federal Government. This is a good program for the banks. They can take this money and allocate it to areas that are in economic need, but that is not what is happening. This money is not going to Cape Breton or to northern Ontario, it is going to the areas which do not need it as much, the areas where there are more companies able to raise funds on their own.
The Government is saying on the one hand that the private sector should be investing in regional development, but on the other hand, we are seeing proof in documents from the government's own agencies that that is just not taking place. As a result, we arc not only losing jobs, but, because of the legislation put forward by this Government, we are losing the legislative infrastructure needed to be able to rebuild the economy.
The Government is saying that it will do away with the industrial development division of Cape Breton Development Corporation. What should have been done instead? Bill C-103, the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Bill, should not have included the abolishment of the industrial development division.
That portion of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency should have been put in Bill C-127 so that the whole question of DEVCO could have been dealt with in one Bill instead of forcing us in the Liberal Party to vote against a Bill that would give funding to Atlantic Canada. Although we find many faults with the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, that was wrong. It was trying to place Members of Parliament in a position of acting against certain areas of Atlantic Canada. That is not the way industrial development is meant to be enacted.
That portion should be in this Bill so we could deal with the whole question. Nevertheless, what is being brought forward for the coal division is appropriate and much needed in view of the fact that the Cape Breton Development Corporation Act was initiated about 20 years ago. This increase from $25 million to $50 million is long overdue.
I ask the Government not to do away with the industrial development division. To do so would be to reduce DEVCO to a coal producing company, subjected to privatization which, of course, will be a consideration of the Government as all Crown corporations are, and thereby cause further unrest and concern
May 17, 1988

in Cape Breton. Surely, Mr. Speaker, this Government has caused enough economic difficulty in Cape Breton without bringing forward further uncertainty with respect to the Cape Breton Development Corporation. To do away with the industrial development division and replace it with Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation will not anywhere near compensate Cape Breton for its loss. First, the industrial development division has its own budget.
Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation will be another arm of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency which already has Enterprise Cape Breton. We have Enterprise Cape Breton. Now we will have Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation. The Government is not even showing the originality of having a different name mainly because it hopes it can gradually merge the two without anyone really knowing. We feel that this is not the time to be doing away with an agency as important as the industrial development division of DEVCO.
I ask that the Government follow through in the spirit in which it is thinking with regard to Bill C-127 by increasing the allotment of the coal division, to consider further the industrial development division of DEVCO and to consider further the economic needs of industrial Cape Breton. By doing this, 1 am sure the Government will then rethink the position on the industrial development division and put a stop to that absolutely silly move it is making which will be very damaging to the economy of Cape Breton.

Mr. Speaker, I am indeed saddened that the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan), a colleague for whom I have great respect, would actually reflect on a vote of the NDP caucus on Bill C-103. He knows perfectly well why we voted for Bill C-103. It had nothing to do with taking moneys away from the people of Cape Breton or indeed from the people of Atlantic Canada. It saddens me because we all know the way things developed in Cape Breton came about not in the last four years of the Conservative Government but came about as a result of years of Liberal rule.
The Liberals were absolutely bankrupt of any ideas other than the patronage approach of Allan J. MacEachen who moved moneys into his riding. That was their big development project. The Liberals' only approach to development with respect to Cape Breton was the shipping out of Cape Breton-ers, people with fantastic capabilities and qualities. They tried to ship them out to other parts of Canada, it was an export of Cape Breton's human resources. When it comes to creative ideas for economic development in Cape Breton, in Atlantic Canada or in northern Ontario, do not look to the Liberals. It is like trying to find eggs in a cuckoo clock. You will not find any. That is why I was saddened by the comments of my colleague.
I just want to say a few words to wrap up Bill C-127. We support this capitalization program. I outlined at the second reading debate the kinds of concerns we had. We tried to reflect the concerns of the people of Cape Breton and the concerns workers of DEVCO had about its future. We tried to get some commitments. I wonder whether the Minister really knew what the Parliamentary Secretary was going to commit himself to. It is on the record. The Parliamentary Secretary was in a committing mood today. He committed everything and I must say what he committed were good things. These are not the kinds of commitments that would run him afoul of the Criminal Code or anything.
To what did he commit himself, Mr. Speaker? He committed himself that every effort would be made to reduce the level of coal dust. He said that if it meant we would have to come back, get more money and capitalization, that this Parliament-and he is quite confident-would not deny increased amounts if that is what it took to reduce the level of coal dust to the accepted two parts per million. He said that the future of DEVCO would continue. He committed himself to that. There was no plan or agenda to downsize DEVCO, to get rid

Railway Safety Act
of it or to close it. That was a commitment. He committed himself that nothing would be done to jeopardize the present DEVCO operation. He committed himself that greater employment opportunities would come as a result of the capitalization included in Bill C-127. He made the commitment that nothing would be done with respect to any other investment in Nova Scotia that would adversely affect DEVCO's operation. He was just a font of commitments.
I hope now that we have the Parliamentary Secretary on the record that he will remember what he said. I hope his Minister does not follow the practice of his Leader who was prepared to say that this is the way it is today but maybe six months later say no, this is not the way it is.
We will support Bill C-127 and the commitments which the Parliamentary Secretary has made on behalf of his Minister and on behalf of the Government. They are now part of the record. We will ensure that those commitments are distributed widely in Cape Breton. We have had the past history of the Liberals, their legacy of disaster in Atlantic Canada and in northern Ontario. Now we have the Conservative commitments. They are on paper. They have been in office for four years and the people of Cape Breton will judge them.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few comments before the debate comes to a conclusion. I have to say at the outset that my colleague, the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), is distorting the facts and history when he makes reference to things that have occurred on the Island of Cape Breton about who was responsible and who was not responsible. I think he clearly and succinctly told us about the lack of appreciation and understanding that his particular Party has for the development of a successful and long-lasting regional economic development policy. In particular, we know what has happened in Cape Breton in the last number of days. The New Democratic Party is running for cover. They are hiding under the tables or in the bushes. They are scared because one of their candidates very clearly agreed with the position of the Liberal caucus concerning ACOA and the industrial development division of DEVCO. We can understand, and I am sure the Parliamentary Secretary can as well, the sensitivity to bruising of the intellectual ego of the NDP.
Who was the candidate?

We have to appreciate their sensitivity because we will run the hell out of them in the next federal election on that issue, not only in Cape Breton but in all of Atlantic Canada. They will have to tell us why they wholeheartedly concur with the philosophy of the Conservative Party of Canada, which is to rack in one agency their entire regional industrial development policy. That is the philosophy, that is the program, that is the intellectual bankruptcy of the NDP on regional economic development. They are sensitive and ought to be sensitive on this important issue.
Regarding Bill C-127 and its substantive provisions, let us not be drunk with delusion. Let us be very candid with one another. This does not provide new working capital, as the NDP and the Government would have you believe, to open up new coal mines in Cape Breton. It is simply a line of credit which has been increased from $25 million to $50 million. Let us not be under any illusions whatsoever that the Government is somehow kowtowing to the interests of the coal miners and the coal industry of Cape Breton. It is emphatically not.
Finally, I do not think any reasonable-and I underline that word reasonable-Member of Parliament could object to this legislation being passed. All it does is amend something that took place some 13 years ago, that being the extension of a credit line. Therefore, I give my concurrence, as does my Party and I believe other Members who have spoken about it. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will in good faith take under active consideration the suggestions and concerns raised in this debate and try and provide at the soonest possible opportunity responses to the real human problems, real human tragedies, involving pensions, pension reform, definition of continuous service, pre-retirement leave, unemployment insurance, job losses, and the terrible insecurity and instability the people in Cape Breton feel over the prospects of the new coal mine in Pictou County. I hope he will give serious consideration to all those concerns as he indicated he would at the outset of the debate.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to hear from the Parliamentary Secretary his remarks

about the members of the committee. We cannot help it if we are so good.

Mr. Speaker, my Party supports the Government's intention to amend the Royal Recommendation to restore the cost sharing formula under the Railway Relocation and Crossing Act which the Bill was originally going to repeal. However, after representations from the Canadian Federation of Municipalities, members of the trade union movement and railway management, as well as members of the committee from all sides, the Government was wise to agree to restore the cost sharing formula for things like grade separation and rail line relocation.
I want to remind the House that, regardless which Party is in power, if we are going to do what needs to be done on grade separation alone we are looking at $200 million a year over the next five years. I know that sounds like a bundle, and it is. However, when we think of what it will save in terms of railway safety in particular and public safety in general and of the fact that we will have put that many more people to work who will pay taxes, we see that it is not all net cost by any means.
This is something which should have been started years ago. It remains to be done yet. The fact that the Government has agreed to retain the cost sharing formula from the old Railway Relocation and Crossing Act makes me a little bit optimistic. It has to do not only with the cost of safety but with the cost of roads and public safety as well.
This legislation also deals, in a somewhat indirect manner, with rail line abandonment as well as rail line relocation which also deals with maintaining maximum safety. Of all the modes of transportation railways are still the safest. When there is a train wreck it is in the headlines, but it is still the safest way to move goods and people.
The Canadian Federation of Municipalities was almost totally ignored on other pieces of legislation. I must be fair and say that the Federation of Municipalities was somewhat lax on other items of legislation. It was not before the Transport Committee when it should have been and it was left up to individual municipalities. However, on this legislation it showed up to represent all the municipalities of Canada.
The Federation made it extremely plain to the Government, through the committee, that it does not want any more transportation of goods transferred from movement by rail to movement by road. My hon. friend, the Parliamentary Secretary, will verify that the Federation was very explicit that it is in no position to provide greater funding not only for maintenance and repair but for construction of additional roadways to handle an ever-increasing amount of truck traffic.
The CPR is presently attempting to abandon 100 miles of track in southern British Columbia, the boundary subdivision.

May 17, 1988
Railway Safety Act
Over 2,000 carloads a year move on that subdivision. The railroad claims it is losing money. Since a truck does not hold as much as a long railway flat car, if that rail line is abandoned it would be safe to say that 3,000 truckloads of traffic will be transferred from the rail on to Highway 3, a narrow, winding road, something which the municipalities of southern British Columbia neither need nor want.
Therefore, safety goes beyond how well railway cars are maintained and constructed and how well track is maintained. I am most pleased that the Government has acceded to the request of the municipalities and members of the committee to retain the cost sharing formula of the Railway Relocation and Crossing Act and to consider rail safety as more than just how safe railway trains operate.
You may be wondering, Mr. Speaker, what this has to do with Motion No. 1 changing the Royal Recommendation. Without changing the Royal Recommendation to restore the formula to up to 80 per cent of the cost paid by the federal Government, not a municipality in Canada would bother to put in a grade separation because they could not afford it. A small municipality could not pay 50 per cent of a grade separation which costs $5 million. It would have trouble paying 20 per cent. It would have to try to persuade the province to pay at least half of that.
A grade separation of eight lanes of traffic and a clover-leaf would cost $20 million, $30 million or $40 million. If this were required in a large municipality, the cost per taxpayer would be as great for a large municipality as for a small one. That is why I commend the Government for its wise decision to retain the cost sharing formula. I would have done more than that. The revolution has not yet arrived, but it will.
That is all I want to say on Motion No. 1. I hope that the Government will proceed to arm the respective Departments and agencies with a number of inspections and enforcement and will assist railways and railway unions to establish good functioning employee assistance programs. Members of the committee from all three Parties were not inclined to obstruct or hold up this Bill. I agree with the Parliamentary Secretary that as a result of the work done in the committee we have a better Bill. It is too bad we cannot do this on a few other Bills.

Mr. Speaker, I support the comments of two of my colleagues who spoke earlier about the exercise we had on the Transport Committee when we were considering this Bill, and I must say it was a most positive experience. We had full co-operation from all Parties, which greatly simplified the Committee's work.
Regarding Motion No. I, to change the maximum grant level from 50 per cent to 80 per cent, I fully agree with this recommendation, especially since it applies to work on construction or alteration of grade separations. Mr. Speaker, it is a fact that most railway accidents happen at grade crossings.
This measure is therefore a very positive one, and I support it wholeheartedly, Mr. Speaker.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I moved this amendment as a safeguard. Even though I have disagreed with several Ministers of Transport over the years, I have found that all of them would not allow precipitous frivolous action to be taken against a citizen. That is the purpose of my amendment.
I do not hesitate to say that this Bill is far from perfect, but no one is perfect. It does not do much about railway safety other than spell out the kind of regulations the Minister or Governor in Council will be able to enact.
I want to thank the Minister and the Parliamentary Secretary for their co-operation and willingness to be guided by a higher wisdom that came from the standing committee and a number of witnesses. The Government was most
Railway Safety Act
prepared to listen and accept reasonable proposals, and accepted some of our amendments during clause by clause study of the Bill.
It was wise to accept about a third of the 25 amendments that the Opposition Members proposed. The other amendments moved by the Government are acceptable, as we have already shown.
1 hope the Government will be equally wise in the consideration of the two amendments moved by myself and the Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), an amendment which he has been trying to pass in the House for a number of years.
The purpose of my amendment is to serve as a safeguard, not only for employees but also lower level management in the railroad. I realize that there are concerns that governments and Parliament should be careful about how much authority under the law they give to Ministers. It has been my experience over the years, watching ministers at both federal and provincial levels, that whenever they abused their power they did not last long. They were either kicked out by their leader or the voters.
One has to trust that a Minister in any portfolio, at any level of government, will use those powers with great discretion. Sometimes they have used too much discretion in exercising their powers.
Clause 41 of the Bill states that anyone who, among other things, violates a rule in force under Clause 19 or 20 is guilty of an offence, punishable on summary conviction. That has never occurred before in transportation legislation. We know that the implementation of these provisions is an experiment.
There is nothing in the Bill in its present form to prevent middle or senior management in a railway company from charging their own employees with violation of company rules. Do not think they would not do it. That was always the case under railway rules before.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with great respect to my colleague, I rise on a point of order. There have been discussions among the Parties. It is approaching five o'clock and I believe you will find unanimous consent not to see the clock so that we can finish this Bill shortly.

Mr. Speaker, for a minute I thought the Parliamentary Secretary did not want me to finish my speech. But I know my colleagues opposite are dying to hear me.
Under the normal railway rules the railway could charge an employee, discipline him, suspend him and bar any raise. This action could only be taken under railway rules. The only other way a railway employee could be charged is pursuant to the

May 17, 1988
Railway Safety Act
Criminal Code. An employee who is proven negligent in a train wreck could be charged with anything from murder to manslaughter, to criminal negligence. I have attended such court cases as a witness.
The purpose of the amendment is to protect employees, not only union employees but lower and middle management employees, from frivolous or malicious prosecutions by overzealous employers.
The second major thrust of this Bill is to put responsibility for railway safety into the hands of the Minister. Railway safety is his first responsibility. The enforcement and application of the legislation is his second most important responsibility. Since the Minister is finally and totally responsible even with respect to something of which he is totally unaware, he is still responsible. If an employee was charged and taken out of service, if he lost pay and had to go to court on what was finally concluded to be a frivolous or malicious charge, then, of course, the court would find so and the employee would be reinstated with back pay and everything else. In the meantime there would have been months and months of grievance procedures, court cases and so on. All this amendment does is ask that the Minister in effect serve as a sort of final adviser to the Solicitor General as to whether or not a charge will be laid under the provisions of this Bill.
The Minister makes the final examination to ensure the change was not frivolous or malicious, and he could say so to the Department of Justice or to the Solicitor General, who would in turn pass it on to a Crown prosecutor. If a railway company on its own volition wanted to lay a charge, that is a different ball game. But under this Act, as it stands, someone in the railway itself could lay a charge. As a protection against frivolous and malicious charges, and also as a protection for whistleblowers, those who point out that such and such happened, I would ask that the Parliamentary Secretary agree with this amendment. It can not do any harm unless we have a bad Minister of Transport, and I do not think he is prepared to admit that. It cannot do any harm but it can do a great deal of good. I hope the Government will accept my amendment.

speakeroldname: Mr. Blaine A. Thacker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt about it, when the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) lays an amendment down, it receives serious consideration because he has had many years of experience in transport, having worked for the railway himself, and he brings a great deal of expertise to this area. I have sympathy for his goal in the sense of him wanting to be able to block the railway companies from maliciously laying charges where he feels it is not appropriate. However, there are some problems with the motion which would state that no charge or complaint may be laid except with the consent of the Minister. Even as late as today I spoke again with the officials in the Department of Transport, who have given the matter a lot of thought. I spoke again personally with lawyers from the Department of Justice.
We believe on balance that the problems that would be created by this type of consent being required of the Minister before a charge could be laid overrules the interests the Hon. Member for Regina West is trying to cover.
There are, according to the officials, very few cases where a political screen is put in before a charge can be laid. That in a sense is what the amendment does. There is one, I gather, in the Official Secrets Act, but that is a matter of high state treason and high state policy under the Canadian Security Intelligence Act. Another example of where it is used is with hate literature under the Criminal Code of Canada. These are very major actions and processes involving the very essence of the state whereas this is a Railway Safety Act. Therefore, the feeling is that it would be unusual to add to this normal statute, if you will, a similar type of political screening.
The normal rule is that the matter would be investigated by the police and by the safety inspectors. Provincial attorneys general might play a role. The federal Attorney General might play a role. However, it is felt that to give that power to a line department Minister, on balance, would be unwise. I ask Members to vote against my friend's amendment even though we respect what he is trying to do. I think there would be other remedies, perhaps in the court itself. Malicious prosecution would be available, perhaps with the court costs.
There would certainly be a remedy through the collective bargaining agreement. If management were to abuse this privilege, there is no doubt there would be hundreds of grievances laid down in other areas. There are all sorts of remedies under the collective bargaining agreement. I think that would be sufficient and I am, therefore, asking Members to vote against the amendment proposed by the Hon. Member for Regina West.

He said: Mr. Speaker, the story behind this amendment began, I guess, in my experience five or six years ago when several of my constituents reported a problem with a fire that had occurred along the main line of the CPR. There were three farmyards that suffered fire damage as a result of a fire that had escaped from the property of the railway.
The farmers made inquiries about compensation. There were several outbuildings burned, one farm and some haystacks at another. The total damage was in the vicinity of $45,000 to $50,000 in terms of property and feed destroyed. They found the CPR very accommodating. They also found that no matter how accommodating everyone was to settle this matter, there was only $5,000 to distribute between the three people who had suffered losses. Thus they received approximately one-third of $5,000 each for an accumulated loss in the area of $50,000.
The problem I found when they complained to me about it was with respect to Section 338 of the old Railway Act. As a
Railway Safety Act
consequence I moved and prepared a motion which, luckily, was drawn and debated in this House which reads in part:
That this House recommend that the Government give serious consideration
to amending Section 338 of the Railway Act to provide for increased
compensation for victims of fire set by railway operations in order to reflect
current replacement costs on items lost through property damage.
Subsequent to a short debate that motion was passed unanimously by the House. Since the Railway Act was recently opened up, I again approached the Government to remind it that it was the will of the House that that particular section be changed to reflect 1986 or 1987 costs. Since it is now 1988 we presume it would reflect 1988 costs, since this $5,000 limit has been in place in the Railway Act since 1903. As the House will know, one dollar in 1903 would buy at least 14 to 15 times more than it will buy today. As a consequence it was suggested that the $5,000 be raised to $75,000 as per this amendment.
There were some subsequent negotiations to attempt to provide an indexing component to this amendment. However, it was found to be very difficult to do something in that order. Thus I fear that subsequent Members of this House 40 or 50 years from now may find that they are having the same difficulty that my constituents had. However, at the moment we are bringing it up to debate with this amendment so that not only will justice be done for those people who have fires in the next year or two, but in fact we will be complying with the wishes of the House of Commons as declared in a motion some years ago.

speakeroldname: Mr. Blaine A. Thacker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, very briefly, I wish to thank members of the committee for the very good work that they put into this Bill. This is part of an overall reorganization of the Department of Transport. It started with Bill C-18, Bill C-19, Bill C-21, Bill C-52, and Bill C-105, which is the final step that will go before the Standing Committee on Transport. It is the Standing Committee that really has done yeoman's service on the part of all three Parties in getting this whole reorganization on transportation law through as public policy for the country.
I always feel that the back-benchers do not receive the credit that they deserve. In this Parliament alone there have been almost 200 bills passed. Yet none of those Bills can get through unless ordinary Members of Parliament sit for hours and hours in committees hearing hundreds of witnesses and then make recommendations to the House as a whole. Backbenchers do not receive enough credit from the public of Canada. I believe that they deserve it.
I am thanking the Members who have worked so hard and diligently on the Standing Committee on Transport.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to comment briefly on Bill C-105. Again, there was full co-operation on both sides when this Bill was considered in committee. The measures proposed in this Bill are long overdue, and it is too bad the accident at Hinton happened before we started this exercise. Mr. Speaker, I welcome the inclusion in this Bill of many of the recommendations of the Foisy Report, such as providing for rest periods, which is already being done. The report's recommendation for a new safety mechanism instead of the dead man's brake has also been implemented. The new system requires some kind of activity in the locomotive compartment, and otherwise the train stops automatically. So this measure has already been put into effect.
Judge Foisy also recommended including a provision that already exists under the Aeronautics Act, namely that physicians disclose any potentially hazardous condition an employee may have. The Bill acts on this recommendation as well. This is a very important measure, Mr. Speaker. The legislation would apply to designated categories of employees. When the employees consult their family doctor, if according to the latter, the patient has a condition that would be a threat to safe operations, he will have to point this out to the medical authorities of the railway company.
We did have some reservations and we wanted to be sure that in this case, the employee would be the first to be notified.
During our discussions in committee, committee members agreed to amend the Bill to ensure that reasonable steps were taken to first inform the person concerned, the employee.
This Bill also tells us that inspection, compliance, and enforcement of railway safety standards will be improved by granting broader powers to inspectors. What the Government does not tell us is that the present number of inspectors is probably not quite adequate. To ensure that safety is taken seriously, the Government will have to provide the necessary funding to employ inspectors in sufficient numbers so that they can carry out their responsibilities. This is definitely a priority, Mr. Speaker.
The report published on the use of drugs by railway employees is a clear indication that we must proceed with certain measures, and everyone seems to agree, employers, unions and workers. I consider it essential that assistance programs be set up for employees who are addicted to drugs or alcohol. That is why, Mr. Speaker, I proposed an amendment to Section 18 of the Bill, which was intended to establish and finance such programs. After discussion in committee, the proposal was reformulated and accepted. I believe that this amendment, Mr. Speaker, was most positive.
The environment is also a subject of concern to everyone; it is of great concern to the members of my party, Mr. Speaker. This Bill may also have an impact on the environment and that
May 17, 1988

is why I have suggested some amendments. For example, paragraph 24(l)(e) of the Bill concerns the removal of trees, brush and weeds on railway lines. I have suggested that alternatives to chemicals be used for this purpose.
I consider this matter to be very important, Mr. Speaker, and I thank the members of the Committee for having kindly accepted this recommendation.
1 also propose that Clause 41 of the Bill be amended in order that heavier fines would be levied in cases of contravention. This was also approved by the members of the committee.
Another matter the committee agreed upon was to ensure that there would be good representation of all concerned groups on the new railway safety consultative committee. This was also agreed to by all members of the committee.
The committee also agreed to retain Section 1 of the Railway Relocation and Crossing Act. Committee members have received numerous representations from municipalities across the country concerned about the loss of section 1. Again, the committee agreed to incorporate this Section in the present legislation.
Over-all the introduction of this legislation, including the measures relating to drug testing, have received widespread support from almost everyone concerned. The task force composed of government officials, the unions, and the railroads did a very good job collaborating with one another and coming out with fairly good proposals for change. All in all, outside of a few measures, the Liberal Party has no problem in supporting this legislation.
As I stated earlier, we will be keeping an eye open to ensure that the Government provides adequate funds to undertake the level of inspection necessary to police the various measures brought forward in this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am inclined to say a few words. Initially, 1 planned on only three minutes, but the Parliamentary Secretary made the mistake of mentioning Bills C-18 and C-19. That revived some bitter memories. He should not have mentioned them. I will not dwell on those at any great length, I promise.
Under the current regime of privatization, deregulation, the trade deal, et cetera, whether it is in the private sector, the public sector, or the Government, everybody states that safety will not be compromised. We have heard that from day one. We heard it as far back as the days of the late unlamented Otto Lang when he was Minister of Transport.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: I hear he is coming back.

Not if I can help it he is not. He is going to try in Saskatchewan, and that is NDP country now.
Railway Safety Act
In terms of rail safety or transportation safety, inspection, maintenance, enforcement, and all the aspects that go into safe public transportation, it does not matter whether it is privately owned, publicly owned, or a combination of both. It does not matter whether it is privately owned in a municipality, or by a municipality, or a provincial government, or a national government. All of them are a public utility, which everyone has to use directly and indirectly. Therefore, no matter what the regime, a national Government has a responsibility that is unavoidable and which it cannot evade.
There have been moves in good directions. This Bill is one of them. The Aviation Safety Board, Accident Investigation Board, is a good move, even though it might have some problems at the moment. There are other areas in which Government and Parliament have moved. But it is not enough to say in a law that there will be adequate inspection and enforcement, that safety will not be compromised unless the law is truly implemented.
I have seen no great moves by the Government or the previous one to increase the number of inspectors, or increase the training of inspectors. In the crucial area of aviation safety we are desperately short of air traffic controllers. It takes three to five years before they are competent to be a controller on their own. We are short of air traffic controllers. All the positions such as air traffic controllers, train dispatchers, locomotive engineers are high stress positions and have to do with safety. They do not have to do with competence. Yet we find a strange dragging of feet on employee assistance programs.
Before I leave the safety matter, I wish to mention that yesterday afternoon I received a long-distance phone call from a lady in Alabama. She is still trying to find out how and why her son was killed in the Gander crash. What does one say? The only thing I can send her at the moment is an article in today's Maclean's magazine. None of us on either side of the House have a darned thing yet that we can say. Her Congressman and Senator have been getting absolutely nowhere. They have been getting roadblocked in the U.S. administration because Canada is not yet ready to tell them anything. She has made appeals to the U.S. Army, and I understand that she may have written to the Government of Canada.
The Aviation Safety Board must conduct inquiries with complete freedom and independence. It must also set up separate inquiries within an over-all inquiry. 1 know that that is the case. There may be an inquiry into icing and de-icing with another inquiry going on about engine failure, and a third one going on about fire on board the aircraft if forensic evidence points to people being dead or unconscious before the crash occurred.
I understand that there is some kind of disagreement or fratricidal war going on about that particular inquiry with the Aviation Safety Board. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary

May 17, 1988
Railway Safety Act
will tell the Minister to sit down with those people and tell them to get their act together, complete the investigation and ensure that it is more than thorough.
1 want Hon. Members to remember and reflect upon the outfit that owned that particular DC-8 aircraft. It was a bad operator. Goodness knows how many times it was charged and fined by the Federal Aviation Administration in the United States following the 1977 deregulation. Deregulation means that the most reputable, safe carrier in any mode, rail, air, or road, is forced to cut corners and to cheat in order to compete. That is why there must be an equity of treatment, enforcement and inspection in all modes of transportation. We cannot do it to one and not do it to the other. This means that the Government has to put in place, by my estimation, 300 to 400 more inspectors for rail, air, marine and road safety.
We have made some great advances in this area, but every year 1 look in the Estimates for an increase in inspectors. Every year I see that the number of inspectors will stay the same or will be decreased because of person-years or the amount of money available.
The proof is in the pudding. There has to be more bucks there. If the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) is having problems with the President of the Treasury Board (Miss Carney) or the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), I invite him to take not only his own colleagues but Members of the Opposition into his confidence and we will all kick them around.
If there is any one increase in taxes that taxpayers will not object to and will in fact applaud, it is an increase in taxes because of increased expenditures in transportation safety, inspection, enforcement and maintenance requirements. I have yet to find a taxpayer, even the most right-wing, wild-eyed Tory, who would object to a few bucks a year more in taxes to do that. The Government need have no qualms about increasing expenditures in that area because there will be no objection from the Canadian people. I said that transportation companies are public utilities, and they are, no matter who owns them.
I would like to say a word about employee assistance programs. During committee hearings, debate and when we discussed the Bill clause by clause, the discussions about the abilities of employees, competent, experienced, trained journeymen, in whatever capacity, got shifted to nothing but alcohol and drug abuse. That is the impression one got. However, there is more to it than that. I think the first priority should be to have employee assistance programs for stress.
If there is stress on the job or off the job which one cannot help but carry to work, it affects one's ability to carry out one's duties because other things are on one's mind and it can also lead to increased use of alcohol or drugs. I think that one is subsequent to the other. I would hope that the Minister would sit down with the railway management and the railway brotherhoods to help them reach a mutual agreement on an employee assistance program.
We can take as a model the program of the Chesapeake and Ohio. We heard a witness from St. Thomas, Ontario, and another from Cleveland, both involved in that railway operation, and we found that that operation has an excellent program which could be a model for our country, not only in the railway sector but in other modes of transportation.
The Minister needs to provide facilities, encouragement, persuasion, arm-twisting and anything else he has to do to have the railway management and the railway brotherhoods reach such a mutual agreement, whether it is a part of a collective agreement or is a separate document. However they want to do it is up to them, but it must be put in place. It can then serve as a model not only for rank and file employees but for management as well in a host of other industries.
Air Canada has in the main set the example for maintenance, safety, inspection and training. It has always been a leader. In fact, it has received international awards on two or three occasions, as I recall, because of that corporate leadership and its efficiency in its dealings with its employees, though there is the odd strike which will happen once in a while.
1 want to illustrate the danger the Government will have to face up to when it comes to deregulation. A reputable carrier, whether it be CNR, CPR, Air Canada or Canadian Air International, is faced with competing with other outfits.
Some new companies have just started up, fly-by-night operations. They face international competition. CP, CN, Air Canada and Canadian Airlines have always had a standard higher than the minimum required by the Government of Canada or the regulatory agency. What we have done now is forced them to bring their standards down to what the Government minimum is. These companies need to be applauded for maintaining standards which are higher than the minimum requirements. Under the kind of regime this Government wants and what is going on south of the 49th parallel, those days are numbered unless and until the Government shows with funding and by example that no carrier publicly or privately owned will be allowed or will be tolerated which does not maintain maximum standards of maintenance, repair, inspection and all the other things that go into the safety of public transportation.
Let me illustrate what position our railroads are now put in because of deregulation. The transportation annex to the trade agreement got dropped, thank goodness. But, under deregulation, Canada will now allow competitive line rates. They are against the law in the United States. An American railroad can then come into Canada, siphon off business from CP and CN under competitive line rates, but CP and CN are not allowed to do the same in the United States. What are those two Canadian railroads to do? They will cut costs. They have to. They have been left no other choice. Two reputable corporations have been left no other choice but to cut costs.
May 17, 1988

When they cut costs, they cut corners and when they cut corners they cut safety. That is the inevitable result with this ideological hysteria and hypnotism of the Tories about deregulation. We are going to go full circle. Mark my words, Mr. Speaker. I plan on being here for several more years. You will see the Government of the day whether it is Tory, Liberal or NDP go full circle and reinstate regulations to make these corporations do what they refuse to do under deregulation or were not allowed to do under deregulation.
Sometimes you need to have regulations, not to stop corporations from doing something, but to make them do something. There is a great deal of difference. I do not think that is Government on somebody's back by having regulations that make corporations do something. It makes them do something in the interests, not only of efficient and safe transportation, but in the interests of the travelling public and in the interests of safety.
1 hope the Government does not think that with this Bill it can rest on its laurels. We will be watching the Estimates very carefully. We will be rising to ask questions in Question Period when there is a shortage of inspectors. We will be raising Cain in the committee and in the House when it is obvious that safety, maintenance and inspection standards have not been complied with or are not at a level where the public can feel as safe as it is possible to feel.
We agree that this legislation should pass today. We hope the Government will proceed with total accident and safety regulations for all modes of transportation with an accident investigation board which covers rail, highway, marine-the whole ball of wax. On the committee I, for one, am prepared to work at this and to work hard. The quicker the better. Let us not rest on this Bill. There is a lot more to be done.

subtopic: MEDICAL RESEARCH COUNCIL-GUIDELINES ON ETHICAL CONDUCT OF RESEARCH INVOLVING HUMAN SUBJECTS
MEDICAL RESEARCH COUNCIL-GUIDELINES ON ETHICAL CONDUCT OF RESEARCH INVOLVING HUMAN SUBJECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) some days back about the guidelines on research involving human subjects, because just at that time the Medical Research Council of Canada had adopted a report dealing with that subject. This document is extremely timely because it raises central issues respecting the protection of human life in society.
The Medical Research Council accepted the report which I hold here as the MRC's guidelines on research involving human subjects. It requires all research funds to be in compliance with these guidelines.
By way of introduction, let me briefly make a few comments about this report and the guidelines. First, it is very clear that this document, and the members of the Medical Research Council Standing Committee on Ethics in Experimentation who authored it are experts in the subject. They come from diverse backgrounds reflecting medical, legal, ethical, theolog-ic, and scientific backgrounds. No one can take lightly the conclusions they come to in the report. I would defer personally to any of them on this subject. I do not raise this subject in

May 17, 1988
Adjournment Debate
Parliament as an expert but simply as a concerned Canadian who sees many straws in the wind and an historic opportunity to weave those straws together into something new, a human life Act.
This document further sets out a fundamental principle on page 12:
The Standing Committee believes that the basic ethical principle in research, as in health care, is respect for life. From this principle flow others: the concept of autonomy, the duty to beneficence, and the duty to justice.
From the principles one quickly gets into the practicalities. We find, for example, on page 32, with regard to research with fetuses and embryos, the following:
At this time, the legal status of embryos and fetuses is not well-defined, nor is the social consensus. While issues of consent and autonomy may not therefore apply, clear ethical concerns arise from the inarguable fact that embryos and fetuses are human life forms.
Finally, I would refer to page 11 of this document which gave rise to my question to the Minister wherein the standing committee states its belief as follows:
... at this time the use of Guidelines within the current body of law is sufficient to reinforce the ethical conduct of research with human subjects.
The significant phrase there is "within the current body of law". It is at this juncture that I submit the Medical Research Council of Canada and those adopting this approach of guidelines only in this difficult area of human experimentation are perhaps pushing an empty wheelbarrow. To say that guidelines will suffice within the body of existing law is to refer to something that truly does not exist. The existing body of law in this area is clearly unsettled.
That is why I advocated on February 4 in this Flouse the formation of a new federal statute which 1 call the human life Act. It would draw together in a single statute all aspects of intentional intervention in the human life cycle.
It would deal not only with the question of abortion, which is so galvanizing this country and this Parliament these days, but with other questions such as genetic engineering, surrogate motherhood, euthanasia, and on and on the list goes. The newspapers are full of it. The Toronto Star of March 29, 1988 had an article headlined "Genetic Tests Open Scary World of Super-Species". The subheading is "Gene-Splicing Promises Society Huge Pay-Offs, But Others Fear Biological Chaos".
We even have the religious press replete with concerns expressed on this subject. For example, the April issue of The United Church Observer had a series of articles under the general heading "Manufacturing a Miracle". One week after I called for a human life Act, the West German Government announced plans to ban research on human embryos, outlaw surrogacy, and curb artificial insemination. The new legislation will forbid surrogate motherhood, production of human embryos for research, measures allowing the choice of a child's sex in artificial insemination, and attempts to breed mixtures of humans and animals.
We have the Canadian Coalition for Reproductive Technologies seeking a royal commission on this subject. It states in its documents that as a society we are not ready to pass laws and that we need first to do the necessary research and engage in a broad, informed national debate. That debate is under way, and I want to see it brought to the floor of the House of Commons in new legislation that can encompass all these questions. The debate will take place this summer at the Fifty-Seventh Couchiching Conference, a well-known national forum for dialogue on public issues. That conference will deal with biological engineering, a blessing or curse.
I have been in touch with David Suzuki who popularizes questions of scientific research in this country. He has gone back to the whole question of genetic engineering and what the Nazis were busy with under the guise of science in Germany in the 1930s. That had as its dimension on one hand the elimination of millions of people, and on the other hand the biological efforts to create a master race. In a letter to me dated May 10, David Suzuki says:
I think you've raised a very important issue and I agree we must not get
bogged down on abortion alone. We have acquired great manipulative powers
that take us into completely uncharted territory. I believe we need a Royal
Commission to look at the issue.
Please press on with your efforts.
Be it a royal commission, be it Bill C-107 dealing with patenting forms of human life, be it the report of the Law Reform Commission, I have much more on this subject that 1 want to bring forward in the discussion. However, given my limited time, I call upon the Government to take a broader initiative at this time and set all this discussion in the framework of a new human life Act.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: MEDICAL RESEARCH COUNCIL-GUIDELINES ON ETHICAL CONDUCT OF RESEARCH INVOLVING HUMAN SUBJECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure it is evident to the Hon. Member as well as others that one cannot address this issue in any depth in the three minutes I have, but I can make one or two points, and that is the purpose of my being here.
First, I want to commend the Hon. Member for his initiative and leadership, not only bringing this issue to the House but also for his efforts in the promotion of a human life Act.
Second, the MRC guidelines are not the first Canadian examination of these issues. It is important to note that this area is moving very quickly for us as a society and as members of the human race. Guidelines are important and they are a good piece of work; they flow from national agreements as well as the summit conference on bioethics which was held in April, 1987. The findings from that conference were taken by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to the Venice Summit a month or two later. No matter the political, ethical, social, or religious make-up of nations, how do we deal with these issues is the question.
The Hon. Member made a very telling point, that the guidelines stress the fundamental importance of respect for human life as the key principle underlining the decisions by researchers and research ethic boards alike, and the difficult
May 17, 1988

ethical decisions intrinsic with human subjects. In conjunction with the guiding principles of justice and of beneficence, this principle, as implemented through the practices developed in these guidelines, ensures that priority in research ethics will be given to protection of human life.
While that assurance is there, I do not think that is a complete answer. The reason I say that that is for the last two years plus is that I have been meeting with groups and asking: "What do we do with respect to developing medical technology? Is our moral and ethical position keeping pace with technology?"
I have said for some time, quite apart from the abortion question and the January 28 decision of the Supreme Court, that I feel personally-and it is difficult for a Minister to put it in that context, but I know the Hon. Member will know what I mean-that we have to explore the possibility of either a royal commission or a ministerial task force to broaden the base and come together as Canadians with a medical system which is considered one of the best in the world, concerning the ethics regarding the preservation of life that are as important a factor as medical technology, experimentation, or the medical breakthroughs we all celebrate.
I cannot go much beyond that other than to commend the Hon. Member and others in this House who have similar viewpoints on the need to explore these questions over the broad range which the Member has brought forward, and I thank him for that.

subtopic: SUFFERED BY MAPLE SYRUP PRODUCERS-POSSIBILITY OF COMPENSATION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
SUFFERED BY MAPLE SYRUP PRODUCERS-POSSIBILITY OF COMPENSATION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject matter is acid rain tonight and specifically concerns the ineptness of the present Government in dealing with Washington. On the one hand one must recognize that the Government of Canada, in the last four years, has completed in a satisfactory manner the negotiations with provincial Governments on the reduction of acid gas pollution. In that way it completed the work initiated by the Liberal Government in 1983-84.
One must conclude at the same time, with a sense of regret, that the foreign policy of the Government on acid rain has been a series of mistakes and failures. We will recall that in 1985 the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) raised the expectations of Canadians by emphasizing that he had a special relationship with President Reagan in Washington and that, on the basis of that special relationship, he would resolve the bilateral problem between Ottawa and Washington and obtain a commitment from the U.S.A. to cut its transboundary pollution.
In 1986 the Prime Minister made a fatal mistake by agreeing to and applauding the recommendation of the acid rain envoys to launch a clean coal technology program over the
Adjournment Debate
next five years in order to accelerate a process of research and demonstration projects south of the border.
I say that was a mistake. The Prime Minister's position on behalf of Canadians should have been that in the United States they should do what they want to do and what needs to be done, but that that which counts for us in Canada is the pollution which comes across the border, and that we want the Americans to join in the signing of the international protocol in Helsinki which requires signatories to cut S02 pollution by at least 30 per cent by 1993.
Having raised expectations in 1985 and given the wrong signal to Washington in 1986, we come to the 1988 Summit and the purpose of my question today. Why at this stage, on the eve of completing the fourth year in office, did the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), and the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) not prepare a bill for damages which we incur yearly as a result of this transboundary pollution?
We have now entered a new phase. We have evidently given up on the special relationship with Washington. We have seen very meagre, if any, results flowing from the clean coal technology program announced and endorsed in 1986. It is, therefore, only sensible to conclude that in the fourth year of the administration, having seen no results from the special relationship and the clean coal technology program, Ottawa would have to use language which is understood in Washington, that is, the yearly presentation of a bill which would indicate the damage caused to Canada by the million of tonnes of pollution which crosses the border into Ontario, Quebec, and the Atlantic provinces.
It is for that reason, that 1 asked this question and prodded the Government. I asked it to prepare such a bill in anticipation of the summit to indicate the damage to our maple sugar producers, the damage to buildings and structures, and the damage to the Muskoka and other resorts, where the losses are reasonably easily quantifiable, where tourist traffic has been affected by the acidification of lakes which has killed the fish in those lakes. The bill should indicate the damage incurred in the growth of our forests, particularly in eastern Canada, as a result of this acidification of soil. It should indicate the damage caused to forestry, to fisheries, and, in some cases in southwestern Ontario, to agriculture.
I admit that in some cases the calculation of the damage may not be easy, while in some cases it may be readily available. Nevertheless, the effort must be made. In this respect we have not developed, even within Environment Canada, the necessary skills because of the cuts in person-years that have been applied as a result of the freeze on its budget. Environment Canada has not even kept up with inflation.
Tonight I want the Parliamentary Secretary to answer in the House the question I asked the Prime Minister. Why is

May 17, 1988
Adjournment Debate
Canada not getting to the point of developing the necessary knowledge and preparing a yearly bill for the damage being caused to our natural resources, to our tourist industry, and to all other facets of Canadian economic and natural resource activities, which it can present to Washington so as to demonstrate to the Americans that we mean business, that we are suffering damage and want compensation. I believe that is a reasonable request, in the fourth year of this administration.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Pauline Browes (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: SUFFERED BY MAPLE SYRUP PRODUCERS-POSSIBILITY OF COMPENSATION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the federal Government is committed to finding a real and lasting solution to the serious environmental and economic damage being caused by acid rain. That is why our Government, unlike the previous Government, has implemented major emission reductions in Canada and has pressed the United States for targeted, mandated emission reductions necessary to stop damage to the Canadian environment.
I want to remind Hon. Members that this Government has been very clear in identifying to United States decision makers and the American public the costs, both environmentally and economically, related to acid rain damage.
More than 350,000 lakes in eastern Canada are vulnerable. Approximately 150,000 lakes have acidity levels at which detrimental effects begin to occur. Some 14,000 have already been acidified, which means they are essentially devoid of normal aquatic life.
More than 50 per cent of eastern Canada's forests grow in areas where rainfall is acidic. More than 80 per cent of all Canadians live in areas where acidic deposits exceed acceptable levels.
In addition to these environmental costs, economically, acid rain is endangering the natural resource base in an area of eastern Canada that measures about 2.6 million square kilometres. This resource base sustains approximately 8 per cent of Canada's Gross National Product and some 250,000 jobs.
We estimate that the annual value of acid rain damage in Canada at approximately $1 billion.
We have told the Americans that we will accept nothing less than an agreement which includes specific emission reduction targets and timetables that will reduce the transboundary flow of sulphur dioxide from the United States into eastern Canada to about two million tonnes in a time frame compatible with our own control program.
If the Hon. Member is suggesting that Canada should be prepared to accept something other than the reductions required to protect our environment, that we might accept money rather than reductions, then I can only say to the Member that the Canadian environment is not for sale at any price. Submitting a bill implies that when it is paid the obligation has been met in full. This Government cannot and will not give the United States a way out of its internationally
recognized obligation not to dump its garbage in its neighbour's yard. This Government is not prepared to sell the Canadian environment, at any cost, as a toxic waste dump site for continuing U.S. acid rain emissions.
CONSUMER AFFAIRS-VIEWS OF RALPH NADER/MINISTER'S POSITION.

subtopic: SUFFERED BY MAPLE SYRUP PRODUCERS-POSSIBILITY OF COMPENSATION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today with respect to a question I put to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) who is often referred to in this place as the Minister responsible for corporate affairs. On August 19, I asked the Minister a question about the high cost of prescription drugs. The Minister, in his wisdom or lack of it, responded in this way, and I quote from Hansard at page 8202:
In Canada we have medicare, and we have social safety nets. Eighty-five per cent of the population is covered by drug plans, including virtually 100 per cent of senior citizens. No one who receives welfare goes without drugs. We have a tremendously beneficial health care system to which Bill C-22 is a positive addition.
This was said by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs for the Government of Canada. I wish to read into the record a letter I recently received from an individual:
1 am writing you concerning the price of prescription drugs. I am a fifty-five year old woman with angina, my husband is a retired veteran on a fixed income, he cannot pay for my drugs on what he receives, and I'm not suppose to work; but had to take a part-time job to pay for my pills. When I started to take "Cardizen", the price was a little over $44.00; now the price is $93.89. The price goes up every two to three months, soon at this rate I won't be able to pay for them with what I make. I cannot get help for this as I'm not old enough.
I am including a copy of my prescriptions from April 4, 1987 to April 11, 1988. There is no reason in this world why the price should go up that much. As far as I'm concerned, it is out and out robbery. I'm bringing this to your attention in hopes that you can do something about it.
That is the kind of letter we in Parliament have been receiving since the Government passed Bill C-22. Both in substance and in its effects, the Bill is causing havoc among those Canadians who do not have the necessary funds to pay for prescription drugs. As was alluded to in previous debates in this House and in committee, the Government has been challenged very vigorously and enthusiastically by Canadians, such as those in the United Church, the Royal Canadian Legion, and six provincial Governments across country. Senior citizens en masse have challenged the Government of Canada that it ought not to proceed with this particular legislation and have indicated that Canadians from coast to coast would have to pay for higher drug prices.
The Government has refused to listen to the calls that have come from all corners of the country. It has reacted in great haste, notwithstanding the enthusiastic opposition we put up in this House, to facilitate multinational corporations in their profit margins while the health of Canadians has been jeopardized.
May 17, 1988

I want to ask the Parliamentary Secretary to explain to Canadian people the rationale for increasing the price of the drug a 55 old woman with angina takes from $44 to $93.89. That is not a 10 per cent increase, nor a 20 per cent increase; it is close to a 102 per cent increase. Is this the justice, the sacred trust, the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) talked about in July, 1984? Or, is this nothing more than a sham that is being put to Canadians by a Canadian Government which seems to be in bed with the multinational corporations?
I suggest, with great sincerity and great respect to you, Mr. Speaker, that Canadians have judged the Government and the actions and words of the Prime Minister. They will come to cast their final judgment in the next federal election. First and foremost on their minds will be the Government's attempt-in fact reality-to sock it to Canadians, to hose Canadians with higher drug prices.
1 would have thought that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs would have regarded his responsibilities as being first and foremost to Canadian consumers. Obviously, that is not his intention. His intentions are to facilitate the profit margins of the multinational corporations, laying aside the health of Canadians and the costs that they will incur in the ensuing weeks, months, and years ahead.
It is unfortunate for a Member to rise in this House to condemn the Government of Canada and all its Members who have aided and abetted this particular process and who have done so without concern for the dignity of those individuals such as the ones I have referred to this afternoon. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary can zero in and focus her attention on this very needy concern for those individuals in Canada who have to pay higher drug prices.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to answer my colleague, especially since I would like to come back to the nub of his question to the Minister concerning Ralph Nader, who as you know is well known as an ardent consumer advocate in the United States.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) answered Mr. Nader's open letter and in his reply, he clearly
Adjournment Debate
stated that the Government of Canada does not set policy based on the recommendations or interests of Americans or of any other country. That is clear. The policy surrounding the drafting of Bill C-22 was made in Canada by Canadians. Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, this policy was made necessary as a result of a commission of inquiry on the pharmaceutical industry in Canada.
People tend to forget. The Hon. Member forgot to mention that his own party, the Government of which he was a distinguished member, had stated that the Drug Patent Act was obsolete and that it had to be changed even if, and I mean even if, it would be hard to get the legislation through.
Mr. Speaker, that is not hard to understand. The Liberals did not have the courage to make this amendment to the Drug Patent Act. They did nothing and we, the Conservative Government, were the ones who had the courage to bring in a bill meeting the needs of all, Canadians as well as drug consumers. The Hon. Member should keep in mind that 85 per cent of beneficiaries in Quebec, and in Canada, have part of their drug costs covered under Medicare and other programs.
The Bill also states that we have a board called ...

The changes to the Patent Act also created the Patented Medicine Price Review Board to ensure consumer protection during the period of market exclusivity given by Bill C-22, and indeed throughout the entire patent life of a drug.

Mr. Speaker, that is clear. The Minister answered the questions raised by our hon. colleague adequately, I think, as he always does, and we agree with him on one point, namely that consumers are entitled to protection and that we are protecting and will continue to protect them; that this party, this Government, is aware of this matter; that the Hon. Member who spoke has done nothing about it. He should congratulate us rather than raise such questions.
